You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

How do these three differ from each other?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read

1	-Hybrid Electric Vehicles
     2	HEVs are powered by an internal combus-
     3	tion engine or other propulsion source that
     4	runs on conventional or alternative fuel
     5	and an electric motor that uses energy
     6	stored in a battery. The extra power
     7	provided by the electric motor allows for
     8	a smaller engine, resulting in better fuel
     9	economy without sacrificing performance.
    10	HEVs combine the benefits of high fuel
    11	economy and low emissions with the
    12	power and range of conventional vehicles.
    13	HEVs do not require a plug to charge
    14	the battery; instead, they charge using
    15	regenerative braking and the internal
    16	combustion engine. They capture energy
    17	normally lost during braking by using
    18	the electric motor as a generator, storing
    19	the captured energy in the battery. The
    20	energy from the battery provides extra
    21	power during acceleration and auxiliary
    22	power when idling.
    23	-Plug-In Hybrid Electric Vehicles
    24	PHEVs are powered by conventional
    25	fuels and by electrical energy stored in a
    26	battery. Using electricity from the grid to
    27	charge the battery some of the time costs
    28	less and reduces petroleum consumption
    29	compared with conventional vehicles.
    30	PHEVs can also reduce emissions,
    31	depending on the electricity source.
    32	PHEVs have an internal combustion
    33	engine or other propulsion source and an
    34	electric motor, which uses energy stored
    35	in a battery. PHEVs have larger battery
    36	packs than HEVs, making it possible to
    37	drive using only electric power (about 10
    38	to 40 miles in current models). This is
    39	commonly referred to as the all-electric
    40	range of the vehicle.
    41	PHEV batteries can be charged several
    42	ways: by an outside electric power source,
    43	by the internal combustion engine, or
    44	through regenerative braking. If a PHEV
    45	is never plugged in to charge, its fuel
    46	economy will be about the same as that
    47	of a similarly sized HEV. If the vehicle is
    48	fully charged and then driven a shorter
    49	distance than its all-electric range, it is
    50	possible to use electric power only.
    51	-All-Electric Vehicles
    52	EVs use a battery to store the electrical
    53	energy that powers the motor. EV batter-
    54	ies are charged by plugging the vehicle
    55	into an electric power source. Although
    56	electricity production may contribute
    57	to air pollution, the U.S. Environmental
    58	Protection Agency (EPA) considers EVs
    59	to be zero-emission vehicles because their
    60	motors produce no exhaust or emissions.
    61	Since EVs use no other fuel, they help
    62	reduce petroleum consumption.
    63	Currently available EVs have a shorter
    64	range per charge than most conventional
    65	vehicles have per tank of gas. EV manu-
    66	facturers typically target a minimum
    67	range of 100 miles. According to the U.S.
    68	Department of Transportation’s Federal
    69	Highway Administration, 100 miles is
    70	sufficient for more than 90% of all house-
    71	hold vehicle trips in the United States.
    72	Light-duty HEV, PHEV, and EV models
    73	are currently available from a number
    74	of auto manufacturers, with additional
    75	models expected to be released in com-
    76	ing years. There are also a variety of
    77	medium- and heavy-duty options avail-
    78	able. For up-to-date information on
    79	available vehicle models, refer to the
    80	Alternative Fuels and Advanced Vehicles
    81	Data Center’s (AFDC) Electric Vehicle
    82	Availability page (www.afdc.energy.gov/
    83	afdc/vehicles/electric_availability.html) and
    84	FuelEconomy.gov.

Based on `doc.txt`, the three vehicle types differ in their power sources, how their batteries are charged, and their electric-only capability:

**Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEVs)**
- "HEVs are powered by an internal combustion engine or other propulsion source that runs on conventional or alternative fuel and an electric motor that uses energy stored in a battery."
- "HEVs do not require a plug to charge the battery; instead, they charge using regenerative braking and the internal combustion engine."
- The battery's role is limited: "The energy from the battery provides extra power during acceleration and auxiliary power when idling."

**Plug-In Hybrid Electric Vehicles (PHEVs)**
- "PHEVs are powered by conventional fuels and by electrical energy stored in a battery."
- Unlike HEVs, they can be plugged in: "PHEV batteries can be charged several ways: by an outside electric power source, by the internal combustion engine, or through regenerative braking."
- They have a larger battery than HEVs: "PHEVs have larger battery packs than HEVs, making it possible to drive using only electric power (about 10 to 40 miles in current models). This is commonly referred to as the all-electric range of the vehicle."
- Their fuel economy depends on charging habits: "If a PHEV is never plugged in to charge, its fuel economy will be about the same as that of a similarly sized HEV."

**All-Electric Vehicles (EVs)**
- EVs have no combustion engine or other fuel: "EVs use a battery to store the electrical energy that powers the motor. EV batteries are charged by plugging the vehicle into an electric power source."
- "Since EVs use no other fuel, they help reduce petroleum consumption."
- "the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) considers EVs to be zero-emission vehicles because their motors produce no exhaust or emissions."
- Their range is more limited: "Currently available EVs have a shorter range per charge than most conventional vehicles have per tank of gas. EV manufacturers typically target a minimum range of 100 miles."

In short, the key distinctions are: HEVs charge only via regenerative braking and the engine (no plug); PHEVs add plug-in charging and a larger battery enabling 10–40 miles of all-electric driving; EVs have no fuel-based propulsion at all, relying solely on a plugged-in battery.
